why: Counting with a frequency map: a transaction changes every copy of oldValue at once, so only its count matters. Keep value -> count and a running sum; each transaction adds (new - old) * count[old] and moves that count to new.
hints: Rewriting the array per transaction is O(n) each, O(n*q) total. Do you need to know where the copies of oldValue are, or only how many there are?
Keep count[value] and total. Replacing old by new changes the sum by (new - old) * count[old].
Then count[new] += count[old] and delete count[old]. Record total after every transaction. O(n + q).
pitfalls: oldValue may be absent: the sum does not change.
oldValue == newValue: do not delete the count after adding it back.
Sums can exceed 32 bits (fine in Python, use long elsewhere).
Merged values stay merged: after 1->4 then 4->2, the former 1s are 2s too.
constraints:
• 1 <= entries.length <= 10^5
  • 1 <= transactions.length <= 10^5
  • 1 <= entries[i], oldValue, newValue <= 10^9
  • The source gives no bounds; these are a reasonable assumption that rules out rewriting the array per transaction.
